questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}+7{y}^{′}+12y=g(x).
$$

The corresponding homogeneous equation has the fundamental solutions ${y}_{1}(x)={e}^{-3x}$ and ${y}_{2}(x)={e}^{-4x}:$According to the method of variation of parameters, we seek a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={{field-1}}
$$

where ${u}_{1}={u}_{1}(x),{u}_{2}={u}_{2}(x),$ that satisfies the constraint

$$
{y}_{p}^{′}(x)={{field-2}}.
$$

Substituting the expressions $y={y}_{p}$ and ${y}^{′}={y}_{p}^{′}$ into the differential equation yields the following relationship between ${u}_{1}^{′},{u}_{2}^{′},$ and $g(x):$

$$
{{field-3}}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a second-order linear inhomogeneous differential equation, the variation of parameters method requires that we seek a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={u}_{1}(x){y}_{1}(x)+{u}_{2}(x){y}_{2}(x)
$$

that satisfies the constraint

$$
{y}_{p}^{′}={u}_{1}{y}_{1}^{′}+{u}_{2}{y}_{2}^{′}.
$$

Here, ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are linearly independent solutions of the corresponding homogeneous equation, and ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are functions to be determined.

In this case, we're told that the fundamental solutions are

$$
{y}_{1}={e}^{-3x},\,{y}_{2}={e}^{-4x}.
$$

Substituting the fundamental solutions into our expression for ${y}_{p},$ we get

$$
{y}_{p}={u}_{1}{e}^{-3x}+{u}_{2}{e}^{-4x}.
$$

Substituting the fundamental solutions into our constraint equation for ${y}_{p}^{′},$ we get

$$
{y}_{p}^{′}={u}_{1}({e}^{-3x})^{′}+{u}_{2}({e}^{-4x})^{′}.
$$

Next, we substitute $y={y}_{p}$ and ${y}^{′}={y}_{p}^{′}$ into the differential equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{″}+7{y}^{′}+12y & =g(x) \\ ({y}_{p}^{′})^{′}+7{y}_{p}^{′}+12{y}_{p} & =g(x)\end{aligned}
$$

Using our expressions for ${y}_{p}$ and ${y}_{p}^{′},$ we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{({u}_{1}({e}^{-3x})^{′}+{u}_{2}({e}^{-4x})^{′})}^{′}+7({u}_{1}({e}^{-3x})^{′}+{u}_{2}({e}^{-4x})^{′})+12({u}_{1}{e}^{-3x}+{u}_{2}{e}^{-4x}) & =g(x) \\ {(-3{u}_{1}{e}^{-3x}-4{u}_{2}{e}^{-4x})}^{′}-21{u}_{1}{e}^{-3x}-28{u}_{2}{e}^{-4x}+12{u}_{1}{e}^{-3x}+12{u}_{2}{e}^{-4x} & =g(x) \\ -3{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{-3x}+9{u}_{1}{e}^{-3x}-4{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-4x}+16{u}_{2}{e}^{-4x}-21{u}_{1}{e}^{-3x}-28{u}_{2}{e}^{-4x}+12{u}_{1}{e}^{-3x}+12{u}_{2}{e}^{-4x} & =g(x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we group all terms proportional to ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}{{(9{e}^{-3x}-21{e}^{-3x}+12{e}^{-3x})}_{⏟}}_{0}+{u}_{2}{{(16{e}^{-4x}-28{e}^{-4x}+12{e}^{-4x})}_{⏟}}_{0}-3{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{-3x}-4{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-4x}=g(x)\end{aligned}
$$

Note that the expressions in parentheses are both zero. Therefore, the equation reduces to

$$
-3{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{-3x}-4{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-4x}=g(x).
$$

Given a second-order linear inhomogeneous differential equation, the variation of parameters method requires that we seek a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={u}_{1}(x){y}_{1}(x)+{u}_{2}(x){y}_{2}(x)
$$

that satisfies the constraint

$$
{y}_{p}^{′}={u}_{1}{y}_{1}^{′}+{u}_{2}{y}_{2}^{′}.
$$

Here, ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are linearly independent solutions of the corresponding homogeneous equation, and ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are functions to be determined.

In this case, we're told that the fundamental solutions are

$$
{y}_{1}={e}^{2x},\,{y}_{2}={e}^{3x}.
$$

Substituting the fundamental solutions into our expression for ${y}_{p},$ we get

$$
{y}_{p}={u}_{1}{e}^{2x}+{u}_{2}{e}^{3x}.
$$

Substituting the fundamental solutions into our constraint equation for ${y}_{p}^{′},$ we get

$$
{y}_{p}^{′}={u}_{1}({e}^{2x})^{′}+{u}_{2}({e}^{3x})^{′}.
$$

We can form a constraint that relates ${u}_{1}^{′}$ and ${u}_{2}^{′}$ by differentiating ${y}_{p}$ and equating this expression to our constraint on ${y}_{p}^{′}.$

Differentiating ${y}_{p}$ with respect to $x$ using the product rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ={({u}_{1}{e}^{2x}+{u}_{2}{e}^{3x})}^{′} \\  & ={({u}_{1}{e}^{2x})}^{′}+{({u}_{2}{e}^{3x})}^{′} \\  & ={u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{2x}+{u}_{1}({e}^{2x})^{′}+{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{3x}+{u}_{2}({e}^{3x})^{′} \\  & ={u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{2x}+2{u}_{1}{e}^{2x}+{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{3x}+3{u}_{2}{e}^{3x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we equate our two expressions for ${y}_{p}^{′},$ and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{2x}+2{u}_{1}{e}^{2x}+{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{3x}+3{u}_{2}{e}^{3x} & ={u}_{1}({e}^{2x})^{′}+{u}_{2}({e}^{3x})^{′} \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{2x}+2{u}_{1}{e}^{2x}+{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{3x}+3{u}_{2}{e}^{3x} & =2{u}_{1}{e}^{2x}+3{u}_{2}{e}^{3x} \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{2x}+\cancel{2{u}_{1}{e}^{2x}}+{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{3x}+\cancel{3{u}_{2}{e}^{3x}} & =\cancel{2{u}_{1}{e}^{2x}}+\cancel{3{u}_{2}{e}^{3x}}\end{aligned}
$$

which finally gives

$$
{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{2x}+{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{3x}=0.
$$

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={u}_{1}(x){y}_{1}(x)+{u}_{2}(x){y}_{2}(x)
$$

that satisfies the constraint

$$
{y}_{p}^{′}={u}_{1}{y}_{1}^{′}+{u}_{2}{y}_{2}^{′}.
$$

Here, ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are linearly independent solutions of the corresponding homogeneous equation, and ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are functions to be determined.

In this case, we're told that the fundamental solutions are

$$
{y}_{1}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\,{y}_{2}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x).
$$

Substituting the fundamental solutions into our expression for ${y}_{p},$ we get

$$
{y}_{p}={u}_{1}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+{u}_{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x).
$$

Substituting the fundamental solutions into our constraint equation for ${y}_{p}^{′},$ we get

$$
{y}_{p}^{′}={u}_{1}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x))^{′}+{u}_{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x))^{′}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ={({u}_{1}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+{u}_{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x))}^{′} \\  & ={({u}_{1}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x))}^{′}+{({u}_{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x))}^{′} \\  & ={u}_{1}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+{u}_{1}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x))^{′}+{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+{u}_{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x))^{′} \\  & ={u}_{1}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+2{u}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)-2{u}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we equate our two expressions for ${y}_{p}^{′},$ and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+2{u}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)-2{u}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x) & ={u}_{1}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x))^{′}+{u}_{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x))^{′} \\ {u}_{1}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+2{u}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)-2{u}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x) & =2{u}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)-2{u}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x) \\ {u}_{1}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+\cancel{2{u}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}+{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)-\cancel{2{u}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)} & =\cancel{2{u}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}-\cancel{2{u}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}\end{aligned}

which finally gives

$$

$$

questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}-{y}^{′}-6y=5\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

The corresponding homogeneous equation has the fundamental solutions ${y}_{1}(x)={e}^{3x}$ and ${y}_{2}={e}^{-2x}.$ 

According to the method of variation of parameters, we should seek a particular solution 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={u}_{1}(x){y}_{1}+{u}_{2}(x){y}_{2}
$$

that satisfies the following constraints:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}^{′}{y}_{1}^{′}+{u}_{2}^{′}{y}_{2}^{′}=5\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{y}_{1}+{u}_{2}^{′}{y}_{2}=0\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Given that ${u}_{2}(x)=-\int g(x)\,\text{d}x,$ find the function $g.$
questions.worked_solution:
We notice that the forcing term is $f(x)=5\operatorname{sin}⁡x.$ Additionally, we're given the fundamental solutions

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{3x},\,{y}_{2}(x)={e}^{-2x}.
$$

First, let's verify that the fundamental solutions ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are independent by computing the Wronskian:

$$
\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}| \\  & ={y}_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}-{y}_{1}^{′}{y}_{2} \\  & =({e}^{3x})({e}^{-2x})^{′}-({e}^{3x})^{′}({e}^{-2x}) \\  & =({e}^{3x})(-2{e}^{-2x})-(3{e}^{3x})({e}^{-2x}) \\  & =-2{e}^{x}-3{e}^{x} \\  & =-5{e}^{x}\ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

Since the Wronskian is not equal to zero, this confirms that the functions ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ are linearly independent. 

Now, we have the following constraints:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}^{′}{({e}^{3x})}^{′}+{u}_{2}^{′}{({e}^{-2x})}^{′}=5\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{3x}+{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-2x}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}3{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{3x}-2{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-2x}=5\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{3x}+{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-2x}=0\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

We wish to find an integral expression for ${u}_{2}.$ We start by eliminating ${u}_{1}^{′}$ from the second equation:

$$
{u}_{1}^{′}=-\frac{{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-2x}}{{e}^{3x}}=-{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-5x}.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{3x}-2{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-2x} & =5\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ 3(-{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-5x}){e}^{3x}-2{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-2x} & =5\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ -3{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-2x}-2{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-2x} & =5\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ -5{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-2x} & =5\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {u}_{2}^{′} & =-{e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}_{2}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int -{e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ {u}_{2} & =-\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that $g(x)={e}^{2x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x.$

questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}-9y={x}^{2}.
$$

The corresponding homogeneous equation has the fundamental solutions ${y}_{1}(x)={e}^{3x}$ and ${y}_{2}(x)={e}^{-3x}.$ 

According to the method of variation of parameters, we should seek a particular solution 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={u}_{1}(x){y}_{1}+{u}_{2}(x){y}_{2}
$$

that satisfies the following constraints:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}^{′}{y}_{1}^{′}+{u}_{2}^{′}{y}_{2}^{′}={x}^{2} \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{y}_{1}+{u}_{2}^{′}{y}_{2}=0\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Given that ${u}_{1}(x)=\int g(x)\,\text{d}x,$ find the function $g.$
questions.worked_solution:
We notice that the forcing term is $f(x)={x}^{2}.$ Additionally, we're given the fundamental solutions

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{3x},\,{y}_{2}(x)={e}^{-3x}.
$$

First, let's verify that the fundamental solutions are independent by computing the Wronskian:

$$
\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}| \\  & ={y}_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}-{y}_{1}^{′}{y}_{2} \\  & =({e}^{3x})({e}^{-3x})^{′}-({e}^{3x})^{′}({e}^{-3x}) \\  & =({e}^{3x})(-3{e}^{-3x})-(3{e}^{3x})({e}^{-3x}) \\  & =-3-3 \\  & =-6\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the Wronskian is not equal to zero, this confirms that the functions ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ are linearly independent. 

Now, we have the following constraints:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}^{′}{({e}^{3x})}^{′}+{u}_{2}^{′}{({e}^{-3x})}^{′}={x}^{2} \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{3x}+{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-3x}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}3{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{3x}-3{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-3x}={x}^{2} \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{3x}+{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-3x}=0\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

We wish to find an integral expression for ${u}_{1}.$ We start by eliminating ${u}_{2}^{′}$ from the second equation:

$$
{u}_{2}^{′}=-\frac{{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{3x}}{{e}^{-3x}}=-{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{6x}.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{3x}-3{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-3x} & ={x}^{2} \\ 3{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{3x}-3(-{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{6x}){e}^{-3x} & ={x}^{2} \\ 3{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{3x}+3{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{3x} & ={x}^{2} \\ 6{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{3x} & ={x}^{2} \\ {u}_{1}^{′} & =\frac{1}{6}{x}^{2}{e}^{-3x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}_{1}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{6}{x}^{2}{e}^{-3x}\,\text{d}x \\ {u}_{1} & =\int \frac{1}{6}{x}^{2}{e}^{-3x}\,\text{d}x \\ {u}_{1} & =\int \frac{1}{6}{x}^{2}{e}^{-3x}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that $g(x)=\frac{1}{6}{x}^{2}{e}^{-3x}.$

\begin{aligned}3{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{3x}-2{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-2x} & =5\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ 3{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{3x}-2(-{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{5x}){e}^{-2x} & =5\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ 3{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{3x}+2{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{3x} & =5\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ 5{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{3x} & =5\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {u}_{1}^{′} & ={e}^{-3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}_{1}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{-3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ {u}_{1} & =\int {e}^{-3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that $g(x)={e}^{-3x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x.$

questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}+3{y}^{′}+2y={x}^{2}.
$$

The corresponding homogeneous equation has the fundamental solutions ${y}_{1}(x)={e}^{-x}$ and ${y}_{2}={e}^{-2x}.$ 

According to the method of variation of parameters, we should seek a particular solution 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={u}_{1}(x){y}_{1}+{u}_{2}(x){y}_{2}
$$

that satisfies the following constraints:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}^{′}{y}_{1}^{′}+{u}_{2}^{′}{y}_{2}^{′}={x}^{2} \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{y}_{1}+{u}_{2}^{′}{y}_{2}=0\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Given that ${u}_{1}(x)=\int g(x)\,\text{d}x,$ find the function $g.$
questions.worked_solution:
We notice that the forcing term is $f(x)={x}^{2}.$ Additionally, we're given the fundamental solutions

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{-x},\,{y}_{2}(x)={e}^{-2x}.
$$

First, let's verify that the fundamental solutions ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are independent by computing the Wronskian:

$$
\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}| \\  & ={y}_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}-{y}_{1}^{′}{y}_{2} \\  & =({e}^{-x})({e}^{-2x})^{′}-({e}^{-x})^{′}({e}^{-2x}) \\  & =({e}^{-x})(-2{e}^{-2x})-(-{e}^{-x})({e}^{-2x}) \\  & =-2{e}^{-3x}+{e}^{-3x} \\  & =-{e}^{-3x}\ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

Since the Wronskian is not equal to zero, this confirms that the functions ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ are linearly independent. 

Now, we have the following constraints:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}^{′}{({e}^{-x})}^{′}+{u}_{2}^{′}{({e}^{-2x})}^{′}={x}^{2} \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{-x}+{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-2x}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}-\,{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{-x}-2{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-2x}={x}^{2} \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{-x}+{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-2x}=0\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

We wish to find an integral expression for ${u}_{1}.$ We start by eliminating ${u}_{2}^{′}$ from the second equation:

$$
{u}_{2}^{′}=-\frac{{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{-x}}{{e}^{-2x}}=-{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{x}.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-\,{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{-x}-2{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-2x} & ={x}^{2} \\ -\,{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{-x}-2(-{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{x}){e}^{-2x} & ={x}^{2} \\ -\,{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{-x}+2{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{-x} & ={x}^{2} \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{-x} & ={x}^{2} \\ {u}_{1}^{′} & ={x}^{2}{e}^{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}_{1}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int {x}^{2}{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\ {u}_{1} & =\int {x}^{2}{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that $g(x)={x}^{2}{e}^{x}.$

questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}-16y=-16\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

The corresponding homogeneous equation has the fundamental solutions ${y}_{1}(x)={e}^{4x}$ and ${y}_{2}={e}^{-4x}.$ 

According to the method of variation of parameters, we should seek a particular solution 

$$
{y}_{p}(x)={u}_{1}(x){y}_{1}+{u}_{2}(x){y}_{2}
$$

that satisfies the following constraints:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}^{′}{y}_{1}^{′}+{u}_{2}^{′}{y}_{2}^{′}=-16\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{y}_{1}+{u}_{2}^{′}{y}_{2}=0\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Given that ${u}_{1}(x)=-\int g(x)\,\text{d}x,$ find the function $g.$
questions.worked_solution:
We notice that the forcing term is $f(x)=-16\operatorname{cos}⁡x.$ Additionally, we're given the fundamental solutions

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{4x},\,{y}_{2}(x)={e}^{-4x}.
$$

First, let's verify that the fundamental solutions ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are independent by computing the Wronskian:

$$
\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}| \\  & ={y}_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}-{y}_{1}^{′}{y}_{2} \\  & =({e}^{4x})({e}^{-4x})^{′}-({e}^{4x})^{′}({e}^{-4x}) \\  & =({e}^{4x})(-4{e}^{-4x})-(4{e}^{4x})({e}^{-4x}) \\  & =-4-4 \\  & =-8\ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

Since the Wronskian is not equal to zero, this confirms that the functions ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ are linearly independent. 

Now, we have the following constraints:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}^{′}{({e}^{4x})}^{′}+{u}_{2}^{′}{({e}^{-4x})}^{′}=-16\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{4x}+{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-4x}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}4{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{4x}-4{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-4x}=-16\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{4x}+{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-4x}=0\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

We wish to find an integral expression for ${u}_{1}.$ We start by eliminating ${u}_{2}^{′}$ from the second equation:

$$
{u}_{2}^{′}=-\frac{{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{4x}}{{e}^{-4x}}=-{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{8x}.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{4x}-4{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-4x} & =-16\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ 4{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{4x}-4(-{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{8x}){e}^{-4x} & =-16\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ 4{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{4x}+4{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{4x} & =-16\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ 8{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{4x} & =-16\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {u}_{1}^{′} & =-2{e}^{-4x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}_{1}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int -2{e}^{-4x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ {u}_{1} & =-\int 2{e}^{-4x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that $g(x)=2{e}^{-4x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x.$

canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
y'' + 5y' - 6y = p(x),
$$

whose corresponding homogeneous equation has the fundamental solutions

$$
y_1(x)=e^{x}, \qquad y_2(x)=e^{-6x}.
$$

According to the method of variation of parameters, we seek a particular solution of the form
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069266/assets/2e180f0d1ea06cd71caafeafb99628fdc8560253293ee5e9375dc84d5b735a64.png)

where $u_1 = u_1(x), u_2 = u_2(x),$ that satisfies the constraint

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069266/assets/32e3388da577fa240b722e46a266b47356239cc79821d7479ed4ea43bd4875d4.png)

Substituting the expressions $y = y_p$ and $y' = y_p'$ into the differential equation yields the following relationship between $u_1', u_2',$ and $p(x){:}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069266/assets/2876b8d3c2d6920da03a828ab411bb489bda9743cc0a210486c725348e14f13c.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Given a second-order linear inhomogeneous differential equation, the variation of parameters method requires that we seek a particular solution of the form

$$
y_p(x) = u_1(x)y_1(x)+u_2(x)y_2(x)
$$

that satisfies the constraint

$$
y_p' = u_1y_1' + u_2 y_2'.
$$

Here, $y_1$ and $y_2$ are linearly independent solutions of the corresponding homogeneous equation, and $u_1$ and $u_2$ are functions to be determined.

In this case, we're told that the fundamental solutions are

$$
y_1 = e^{x}, \qquad y_2 = e^{-6x}.
$$

Substituting the fundamental solutions into our expression for $y_p,$ we get

$$
y_p =u_1e^{x}+u_2e^{-6x}.
$$

Substituting the fundamental solutions into our constraint equation for $y_p',$ we get

$$
y_p' =u_1(e^{x})'+u_2 (e^{-6x})'.
$$

Next, we substitute $y = y_p$ and $y' = y_p'$ into the differential equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{″}+5{y}^{′}-6y & =p(x) \\ ({y}_{p}^{′})^{′}+5{y}_{p}^{′}-6{y}_{p} & =p(x)\end{aligned}
$$

Using our expressions for $y_p$ and $y_p',$ we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{({u}_{1}({e}^{x})^{′}+{u}_{2}({e}^{-6x})^{′})}^{′}+5({u}_{1}({e}^{x})^{′}+{u}_{2}({e}^{-6x})^{′})-6({u}_{1}{e}^{x}+{u}_{2}{e}^{-6x}) & =p(x) \\ {({u}_{1}{e}^{x}-6{u}_{2}{e}^{-6x})}^{′}+5{u}_{1}{e}^{x}-30{u}_{2}{e}^{-6x}-6{u}_{1}{e}^{x}-6{u}_{2}{e}^{-6x} & =p(x) \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{x}+{u}_{1}{e}^{x}-6{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-6x}+36{u}_{2}{e}^{-6x} \\ \,+5{u}_{1}{e}^{x}-30{u}_{2}{e}^{-6x}-6{u}_{1}{e}^{x}-6{u}_{2}{e}^{-6x} & =p(x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we group all terms proportional to $u_1$ and $u_2{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}{{({e}^{x}+5{e}^{x}-6{e}^{x})}_{⏟}}_{0}+{u}_{2}{{(36{e}^{-6x}-30{e}^{-6x}-6{e}^{-6x})}_{⏟}}_{0}+{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{x}-6{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-6x}=p(x)\end{aligned}
$$

Note that the expressions in parentheses are both zero. Therefore, the equation reduces to

$$
u_1'e^{x} - 6u_2'e^{-6x} = p(x).
$$

where $u_1 = u_1(x), u_2 = u_2(x),$ that satisfies the constraint

Differentiating $y_p$ with respect to $x,$ we obtain

Therefore, we have the following constraint equation relating $u_1'$ and $u_2'{:}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069266/assets/2876b8d3c2d6920da03a828ab411bb489bda9743cc0a210486c725348e14f13c.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Given a second-order linear inhomogeneous differential equation, the variation of parameters method requires that we seek a particular solution of the form

$$
y_p(x) = u_1(x)y_1(x)+u_2(x)y_2(x)
$$

that satisfies the constraint

$$
y_p' = u_1y_1' + u_2 y_2'.
$$

Here, $y_1$ and $y_2$ are linearly independent solutions of the corresponding homogeneous equation, and $u_1$ and $u_2$ are functions to be determined.

In this case, we're told that the fundamental solutions are

$$
y_1 = \sin(4x), \qquad y_2 = \cos(4x).
$$

Substituting the fundamental solutions into our expression for $y_p,$ we get

$$
y_p =u_1\sin(4x)+u_2\cos(4x).
$$

Substituting the fundamental solutions into our constraint equation for $y_p',$ we get

$$
y_p' = u_1(\sin(4x))'+u_2 (\cos(4x))'.
$$

We can form a constraint that relates $u_1'$ and $u_2'$ by differentiating $y_p$ and equating this expression to our constraint on $y_p'.$

Differentiating $y_p$ with respect to $x$ using the product rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ={({u}_{1}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)+{u}_{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x))}^{′} \\  & ={({u}_{1}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x))}^{′}+{({u}_{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x))}^{′} \\  & ={u}_{1}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)+{u}_{1}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x))^{′}+{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)+{u}_{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x))^{′} \\  & ={u}_{1}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)+4{u}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)+{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)-4{u}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we equate our two expressions for $y_p',$ and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)+4{u}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)+{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)-4{u}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x) & ={u}_{1}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x))^{′}+{u}_{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x))^{′} \\ {u}_{1}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)+4{u}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)+{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)-4{u}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x) & =4{u}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)-4{u}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x) \\ {u}_{1}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)+\cancel{4{u}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)}+{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)-\cancel{4{u}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)} & =\cancel{4{u}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)}-\cancel{4{u}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)}\end{aligned}
$$

which finally gives

$$
u_1' \sin(4x) + u_2' \cos(4x) = 0.
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
y'' + 9y = 6\cos x.
$$

The corresponding homogeneous equation has the fundamental solutions $y_1(x) = \cos(3x)$ and $y_2 = \sin(3x).$ 

According to the method of variation of parameters, we should seek a particular solution 

$$
y_p(x) = u_1(x) y_1 + u_2(x) y_2
$$

that satisfies the following constraints:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}^{′}{y}_{1}^{′}+{u}_{2}^{′}{y}_{2}^{′}=6\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{y}_{1}+{u}_{2}^{′}{y}_{2}=0\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Given that $\displaystyle u_2(x) = \int g(x)\,\textrm d x,$ find the function $g.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We notice that the forcing term is $f(x) = 6\cos x.$ Additionally, we're given the fundamental solutions

$$
y_1(x) = \cos(3x), \qquad y_2(x) = \sin(3x).
$$

First, let's verify that the fundamental solutions $y_1$ and $y_2$ are independent by computing the Wronskian:

$$
\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}| \\  & ={y}_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}-{y}_{1}^{′}{y}_{2} \\  & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))(\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x))^{′}-(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))^{′}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)) \\  & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))(3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))-(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x))(\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)) \\  & =3{cos}^{2}⁡(3x)+3{sin}^{2}⁡(3x) \\  & =3\ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

Since the Wronskian is not equal to zero, this confirms that the functions $y_1(x)$ and $y_2(x)$ are linearly independent. 

Now, we have the following constraints:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}^{′}{(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))}^{′}+{u}_{2}^{′}{(\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x))}^{′}=6\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {u}_{1}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)+{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}-3{u}_{1}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)+3{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)=6\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {u}_{1}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)+{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)=0\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

We wish to find an integral expression for $u_2.$ We start by eliminating $u_1'$ from the second equation:

$$
u_1' = -\dfrac{u_2'\sin(3x)}{\cos(3x)}.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-3{u}_{1}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)+3{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x) & =6\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ -3(-\frac{{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)})\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)+3{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x) & =6\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ 3{u}_{2}^{′}\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡(3x)}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}+3{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x) & =6\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ 3{u}_{2}^{′}\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡(3x)+{cos}^{2}⁡(3x)}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)} & =6\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ 3{u}_{2}^{′}\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)} & =6\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {u}_{2}^{′} & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x).\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}_{2}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int 2\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\ {u}_{2} & =\int 2\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that $g(x) = 2\cos x \cos(3x).$
